<CalloutBox type="most-tested">
The distinction between Le Corbusier's functionalism and Mies van der Rohe's minimalism appears in nearly every LEA History/Theory exam cycle. Focus on: Corbusier's Five Points vs Mies' Universal Space — these two architects represent opposite poles of modernism and their contrast is a perennial exam favorite.
</CalloutBox>

blocks.raw: <Tip>The exact quote is "A house is a machine for living in" (not "to live in"; not "living machine"). This precise wording is frequently tested. The phrasing emphasizes *function*, not emotion—machines are tools, not homes in the sentimental sense. Le Corbusier is NOT saying houses are cold; he's saying function comes first, then beauty emerges from proportion and order.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Note>Five Points are testable individually and combined. Be able to: (1) list all five, (2) explain each one's functional benefit (pilotis = ground permeability, free plan = flexible interior use), (3) show how Five Points enable mass production. They are not merely aesthetic; they are structural-functional principles enabling replicable design systems.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Le Corbusier is NOT Mies van der Rohe. Both are modernists but fundamentally opposed. Le Corbusier = utopian mass production + geometric idealism + social housing ambition. Mies = universal flexible space + material reduction + individual expression. The most common LEA error is citing them interchangeably. They are poles of modernism.</Warn>

blocks.raw:
<Callout>

Modernist architecture is dominated by a small number of visionary architects whose philosophies are *extensively tested* on the LEA through quote-to-architect matching, identification of theoretical concepts, and analysis of key works. The LEA tests exact attribution of famous quotes—Le Corbusier's "A house is a machine for living," Mies van der Rohe's "Less is more," Louis Sullivan's "Form follows function," and dozens of others. You must know the precise wording of each quote and its correct architect, as distractor options will include misattributions and paraphrases. This section consolidates verified quote attributions and philosophical frameworks.
</Callout>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Reversing Le Corbusier and Mies's Philosophies. Students sometimes conflate them because both are modernists. Key distinction: Le Corbusier embraced geometric idealism, mass production (Modulor, Maison Domino), and utopian social vision. Mies pursued extreme reduction, universal space, and material honesty. They are opposite poles of modernism.", "Misquoting \"A house is a machine for living\". Common errors include:
   - \"A house is a machine to *live* in\" (incorrect word choice; it's \"*living*\")
   - Attributing it to Mies or Adolf Loos instead of Le Corbusier
   - Misremembering it as \"A home is...\" or \"Architecture is...\"", "Oversimplifying \"Ornament and Crime\". Students sometimes think Loos banned all aesthetics. In fact, Loos opposed *unnecessary decorative ornamentation* and valued craftsmanship, material beauty, and proportion. He wasn't against beauty—against wasteful ornament.", "Forgetting the Expresionist Alternative. Students focused on Le Corbusier and Mies (rationalist, minimalist) sometimes overlook Erich Mendelsohn's Expressionism, which valued dynamic form and emotional spatial experience. The LEA may test this as a third modernist position.", "Confusing Aalto with Other Modernists. Alvar Aalto's humanist modernism—organic curves, natural materials, warmth—is frequently misattributed to Wright (organic architecture) or confused with functionalism. Key distinction: Aalto humanized modernism; he wasn't anti-modern, but anti-cold-minimalism.", "Misattributing Wright's Organic Architecture to Modernism Generally. Frank Lloyd Wright's philosophy predates and differs from European modernism. His organic architecture is not the same as Le Corbusier's functionalism or Mies's minimalism. Wright's roots are in nature and site; European modernists' roots are in industry and rationality.", "Forgetting Gropius's Educational Philosophy. Students know the Bauhaus as a design school but miss Gropius's specific pedagogical contribution: uniting art, craft, and technology through the workshop model. The phrase \"The school is the servant of the workshop\" distinguishes his approach from academic theory-only teaching.", "Misunderstanding Buckminster Fuller's \"Design Science\". Students may confuse it with Le Corbusier's functionalism. Fuller's Design Science is systems-thinking, anticipatory, global resource optimization. Le Corbusier's is utopian mass production. Fuller thought in terms of geodesic domes and Dymaxion geometry; Le Corbusier thought in terms of standardized housing units."]} />

   - Attributing it to Mies or Adolf Loos instead of Le Corbusier
   - Misremembering it as \"A home is...\" or \"Architecture is...\"", "Oversimplifying \"Ornament and Crime\". Students sometimes think Loos banned all aesthetics. In fact, Loos opposed *unnecessary decorative ornamentation* and valued craftsmanship, material beauty, and proportion. He wasn't against beauty—against wasteful ornament.", "Forgetting the Expresionist Alternative. Students focused on Le Corbusier and Mies (rationalist, minimalist) sometimes overlook Erich Mendelsohn's Expressionism, which valued dynamic form and emotional spatial experience. The LEA may test this as a third modernist position.", "Confusing Aalto with Other Modernists. Alvar Aalto's humanist modernism—organic curves, natural materials, warmth—is frequently misattributed to Wright (organic architecture) or confused with functionalism. Key distinction: Aalto humanized modernism; he wasn't anti-modern, but anti-cold-minimalism.", "Misattributing Wright's Organic Architecture to Modernism Generally. Frank Lloyd Wright's philosophy predates and differs from European modernism. His organic architecture is not the same as Le Corbusier's functionalism or Mies's minimalism. Wright's roots are in nature and site; European modernists' roots are in industry and rationality.", "Forgetting Gropius's Educational Philosophy. Students know the Bauhaus as a design school but miss Gropius's specific pedagogical contribution: uniting art, craft, and technology through the workshop model. The phrase \"The school is the servant of the workshop\" distinguishes his approach from academic theory-only teaching.", "Misunderstanding Buckminster Fuller's \"Design Science\". Students may confuse it with Le Corbusier's functionalism. Fuller's Design Science is systems-thinking, anticipatory, global resource optimization. Le Corbusier's is utopian mass production. Fuller thought in terms of geodesic domes and Dymaxion geometry; Le Corbusier thought in terms of standardized housing units."]}
